{{Short description|Theorem about circles}}
{{For|the "butterfly lemma" of group theory|Zassenhaus lemma}}

[[File:Butterfly theorem.svg|upright=1.0|thumb|{{center|Butterfly theorem:}}
{{center|{{mvar|M}} is the midpoint of {{mvar|{{overline|XY}}}}.}}]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''butterfly theorem''' is a classical result which can be stated as follows:<ref name=Johnson>Johnson, Roger A., ''Advanced Euclidean Geometry'', Dover Publ., 2007 (orig. 1929).</ref>{{rp|p. 78}}

Let {{mvar|M}} be the [[midpoint]] of a [[Chord (geometry)|chord]] {{mvar|{{overline|PQ}}}} of a [[circle]], through which two other chords {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}} are drawn; {{mvar|{{overline|AD}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} intersect chord {{mvar|{{overline|PQ}}}} at {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} correspondingly. Then {{mvar|M}} is the midpoint of {{mvar|{{overline|XY}}}}.

==Proof==
[[File:Butterfly1.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|{{center|Proof of Butterfly theorem}}
{{legend-line|solid red 2px|Chord {{mvar|{{overline|PQ}}}} with known midpoint {{mvar|M}}.}}
{{legend-line|solid magenta 2px|Perpendiculars from {{mvar|Y}}.}}
{{legend-line|solid cyan 2px|Perpendiculars from {{mvar|X}}.}}
{{legend-line|solid lime 2px|Chords intersecting {{mvar|{{overline|PQ}}}} at {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}}, and {{mvar|M}}.}}
To be proved: {{math|1=''{{overline|MX}}'' = ''{{overline|MY}}''}}.
]]

A formal proof of the theorem is as follows:
Let the [[perpendiculars]] {{mvar|{{overline|XX′}}}}  and {{mvar|{{overline|XX″}}}} be dropped from the point {{mvar|X}} on the straight lines {{mvar|{{overline|AM}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|DM}}}} respectively. Similarly, let {{mvar|{{overline|YY′}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|YY″}}}} be dropped from the point {{mvar|Y}} perpendicular to the straight lines {{mvar|{{overline|BM}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|CM}}}} respectively.

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \triangle MXX' &\sim \triangle MYY', \\[2pt]
  \therefore {\overline{MX} \over \overline{MY}} &= {\overline{XX'} \over \overline{YY'}}. \\[8pt]
 
  \triangle MXX'' &\sim \triangle MYY'', \\[2pt]
  \therefore {\overline{MX} \over \overline{MY}} &= {\overline{XX''} \over \overline{YY''}}. \\[8pt]
 
  \triangle AXX' &\sim \triangle CYY'', \\[2pt]
  \therefore {\overline{XX'} \over \overline{YY''}} &= {\overline{AX} \over \overline{CY}}. \\[8pt]
 
  \triangle DXX'' &\sim \triangle BYY', \\[2pt]
  \therefore {\overline{XX''} \over \overline{YY'}} &= {\overline{DX} \over \overline{BY}}. 
\end{align}</math>

From the preceding equations and the [[intersecting chords theorem]], it can be seen that

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \left({\overline{MX} \over \overline{MY}}\right)^2 &= {\overline{XX'} \over \overline{YY'}} \cdot {\overline{XX''} \over \overline{YY''}}, \\[2pt]
  &= {\overline{AX} \cdot \overline{DX} \over \overline{CY} \cdot \overline{BY}}, \\[2pt]
  &= {\overline{PX} \cdot \overline{QX} \over \overline{PY} \cdot \overline{QY}}, \\[2pt]
  &= { \bigl(\overline{PM} - \overline{XM} \bigr) \cdot \bigl(\overline{MQ} + \overline{XM}\bigr) \over \bigl(\overline{PM} + \overline{MY}\bigr) \cdot \bigl(\overline{QM} - \overline{MY}\bigr)}, \\[2pt]
  &= { \overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MX}^2 \over \overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MY}^2}, \end{align}</math>

since {{math|''{{overline|PM}}'' {{=}} ''{{overline|MQ}}''}}. Thus,

<math display=block> { \overline{MX}^2 \over \overline{MY}^2} = {\overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MX}^2 \over \overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MY}^2}. </math>

Cross-multiplying the latter equation and cancelling out common terms,

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \overline{MX}^2 \cdot \overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MX}^2 \cdot \overline{MY}^2 &= \overline{MY}^2 \cdot \overline{PM}^2 - \overline{MX}^2 \cdot \overline{MY}^2, \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad \overline{MX}^2 \cdot \overline{PM}^2 &= \overline{MY}^2 \cdot \overline{PM}^2, \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad \overline{MX}^2 &= \overline{MY}^2, \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad \overline{MX} &= \overline{MY}.
\end{align}</math>

Thus, {{mvar|M}} is the midpoint of {{mvar|{{overline|XY}}}}.

Other proofs exist,<ref>Martin Celli, "A Proof of the Butterfly Theorem Using the Similarity Factor of the Two Wings", ''[[Forum Geometricorum]]'' 16, 2016, 337–338. http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2016volume16/FG201641.pdf</ref> including one using [[projective geometry]].<ref>[http://www.imomath.com/index.php?options=628&lmm=0], problem 8.</ref>

==History==
Proving the butterfly theorem was posed as a problem by [[William Wallace (mathematician)|William Wallace]] in ''The Gentleman's Mathematical Companion'' (1803). Three solutions were published in 1804, and in 1805 [[Sir William Herschel]] posed the question again in a letter to Wallace. Reverend Thomas Scurr asked the same question again in 1814 in the ''Gentleman's Diary or Mathematical Repository''.<ref>[http://www.cut-the-knot.org/pythagoras/WallaceButterfly.shtml William Wallace's 1803 Statement of the Butterfly Theorem], [[cut-the-knot]], retrieved 2015-05-07.</ref>
